narrative: Your profile was assessed as having a 73% likelihood of leaving, which is why the promotion was denied: the model treats a high chance of departure as a risk that the role may soon need to be filled again. The strongest signal was your overall work experience. At 6–10 years, you fall into a group that is less common among employees predicted to stay, where about half have only 1–5 years, and this pushed the estimate toward leaving. Next, you indicated that you have received other job opportunities while in this job. That is relatively uncommon among predicted stayers—roughly three-quarters said no—and it was the second-strongest push toward leaving. Third, your tenure in the current organization is 1–5 years. Although this range is common among stayers, in your combination of circumstances the model weighed it as another factor raising departure risk. These three factors outweighed the stabilizing signals in your profile. Before reconsidering promotion, it would be useful to discuss your career path, whether external opportunities are being actively considered, and what retention support—such as clearer progression, development, or recognition—would make staying and advancing mutually attractive. A conversation about commitment and future roles can clarify whether the departure risk is real or can be reduced.
